title: Kernel, image, and rank-nullity
section: Linear Transformations ▷ The Rank Plus Nullity Theorem
terms: kernel; range; image; nullity; rank-nullity theorem; injective linear map; surjective linear map; isomorphism.

exposition.text:
The kernel of T : V → W is {v : T (v) = 0}, and its image or range is {T (v) : v ∈ V }. Both are
subspaces, respectively of the domain and codomain. Their dimensions are the nullity and rank.
For finite-dimensional V , dim ker T + dim im T = dim V .
A linear map is injective exactly when its kernel is zero and surjective exactly when its image
equals the codomain. With equal finite domain and codomain dimensions, injectivity and sur-
jectivity are equivalent. A bijective linear map is an isomorphism. These conclusions need the
correct dimension: subtract nullity from the domain dimension, not from the codomain dimen-
sion.
For a subspace U ⊆ V , the restricted map has kernel U ∩ ker T , so dim T (U ) = dim U − dim(U ∩
ker T) when U is finite dimensional. Infinite-dimensional endomorphisms can be surjective
without being injective, or conversely; differentiation and multiplication by x on polynomial
spaces provide the two examples.

question.text:

A linear map T : R → R has a four-dimensional kernel. Which is necessarily true?
(A) It is onto
(B) It is one-to-one
(C) Its image has dimension 3
(D) Its image has dimension 4
(E) Its image has dimension 5

solution.text:
Rank-nullity gives rank 7 − 4 = 3. Thus it is neither injective nor surjective, and its image is
5
a three-dimensional subspace of R .

question.text:
On the vector space R[x] of all real polynomials, differentiation D is
(A) injective and surjective
(B) injective but not surjective
(C) surjective but not injective
(D) neither injective nor surjective
(E) not a linear map

solution.text:
Every polynomial has a polynomial antiderivative, so differentiation is onto. Its kernel
consists of constant polynomials and is nontrivial, so it is not one-to-one. Equal domain
and codomain do not make injectivity and surjectivity equivalent in an infinite-dimensional
space.

question.text:
5 3 5
A linear map T : R → R has rank three. As U ranges over four-dimensional subspaces of R ,
which values can dim T(U) take?
(A) Only 1 (B) Only 2 (C) Only 3 (D) 1 or 2 (E) 2 or 3

solution.text:
The kernel has dimension two. Its intersection with U has dimension at least 4 + 2 − 5 = 1
and at most two. Rank-nullity for the restriction gives dim T(U) = 4 − dim(U ∩ ker T), hence
two or three. A basis adapted to the kernel constructs subspaces attaining either value.

question.text:
3
Define E : P → R by E(p) = (p(0), p(1), p(2)). Which statement is correct?
2
(A) E is an isomorphism.
(B) E is onto but has a one-dimensional kernel.
(C) E is one-to-one but not onto.
(D) E has rank two.
(E) E is not linear because evaluation changes the argument.

solution.text:
Evaluation is linear. If E(p) = 0, then a polynomial of degree at most two has three dis-
tinct roots, so p = 0. The kernel is trivial. Both spaces have dimension three, hence injec-
tivity implies surjectivity and E is an isomorphism.
